courses.title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
courses.imageAlt: Illustration: Bit, the course's robot, learning a route through a small gridworld to a goal star
paragraphs: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning is Teddy Lazebnik's free course on how an agent learns to act by trying things and seeing what happens. It has 12 lectures, each with slides written to be read on your own, 51 short animated episodes with full transcripts, nine interactive labs and three games, all running in your browser.

The course starts with the agent–environment loop, rewards, returns and values, then studies the trade-off between exploring and exploiting through the multi-armed bandit. From there it builds Markov decision processes and dynamic programming, with a lecture on why the Bellman operators converge, before learning without a model: Monte Carlo, temporal-difference learning, SARSA and Q-learning. The second half scales up to function approximation and deep Q-networks, planning with learned models and Monte Carlo tree search, policy gradients and actor-critics, learning many things from one stream of experience, and finally learning from people, from imitation and inverse RL to the Bradley–Terry model and RLHF.

Every lecture page puts its slides, episodes and matching lab or game in one place, so you can watch an idea, read it properly and then try it yourself. Bit, the course's little robot, learns alongside you.

courses.title: Epidemic Modeling
courses.imageAlt: Illustration: a toy town where an infection passes between people, next to the curves of a simple SIR epidemic
paragraphs: Epidemic Modeling is Teddy Lazebnik's free course on how mathematical and computational models describe, forecast and help control the spread of infectious diseases. It follows his book, Epidemic Modeling: Principles, Algorithms, and Applications (Academic Press, 2026), across 13 modules, with 53 short animated episodes, slide decks for 12 modules, 11 interactive labs and a game, all in our own words, figures and simulations.

It opens with history, from the plagues that shaped societies to 1918 and COVID-19, and with the biology, behavior and politics that drive spread. The core builds the SIR model from scratch, the meaning of R₀ and the next-generation matrix, then adds more states and classes, changing transmission and the role of chance. Next come cities linked by travel, contact networks and continuous space, competing and mutating strains, and agent-based simulation. The later modules turn to data and decisions: data-driven models, parameter estimation and calibration, surveillance, mobility and genomic data, intervention policies, uncertainty and sensitivity analysis, and the computing behind it all.
Each module page brings its episodes, slides and labs together. The episodes are released module by module.

courses.title: Symbolic Physical Laws Discovery
courses.imageAlt: Illustration: the expression tree of a·exp(−k·t) and the curve it draws through measured points, marked as a candidate law
paragraphs: Symbolic Physical Laws Discovery is Teddy Lazebnik's free course on discovering physical laws with computers. It follows his forthcoming book, Computational Methods for Symbolic Physical Laws Discovery, across 10 modules, each with long animated videos of ten to fifteen minutes, a slide deck written to be read on your own and a lab that runs in your browser, all in our own words, figures and simulations.

It starts with why science wants equations and not only good predictions, then shows how formulas are written as data, how units, symmetries and known physics enter the search, and how enumeration and genetic programming move through equation space. Later modules cover the data a discovery needs, static laws and surrogates, differential equations, laws in space and time, how far a discovered law can be trusted, and where the field is going.
Modules go online one at a time: 10 module pages are up with their slides and 10 labs, and the videos are published as each one is finished.

courses.title: Computational Approaches to the Non-Observed Economy
courses.imageAlt: Illustration: a small map of districts shaded by how much activity goes unrecorded, beside bars for what was produced and what was recorded
paragraphs: Computational Approaches to the Non-Observed Economy is Teddy Lazebnik's free course on studying what official statistics miss: informal, underground, illegal and unrecorded production. It follows the forthcoming book of the same name across 9 modules, each with long animated videos with full transcripts, a slide deck written to be read on your own, and a lab that runs in your browser.

It starts with who observes what and why the size of the hidden economy depends on its definition, then builds theory-driven and data-driven models of a target nobody sees, games between auditors and the people they audit, estimates of the size with honest errors, forecasts that survive drift, maps and networks, agent-based towns where hiding emerges by itself, and policy chosen under uncertainty. It ends with a practical guide from a question to a defensible answer. The towns and countries are invented, so every method can be checked against a known truth.
Modules go online one at a time: 9 module pages are up with their slides and 9 labs, and the videos are published as each one is finished.
